title: A pricing page for a small clinic
metaTitle: A small clinic pricing page patients can read
excerpt: A clinic pricing page should show what a visit includes, what it does not, and the shape of the fee, then let an anxious patient book without a surprise.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, a structure you can read from the street, for a pricing page that should be just as legible.
caption: A white building with a glass wing. The fee should be this easy to read from outside. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a small clinic publish its fees?
faqs.answer: Publish the fees your front desk already says out loud, especially the first visit. Patients use the page to judge whether they can come, not to do long arithmetic. If a fee truly depends on an examination, say what the first visit costs and what might be recommended afterward. "Call for pricing" on a knowable fee reads like a surprise.

faqs.question: How should insurance be described?
faqs.answer: Say whether you bill insurance, whether the patient pays you and claims back, or whether you are self-pay only, and name the plans only if the list is current. Explain what the patient should bring. Do not imply a plan will pay for a visit if you have not checked. The shape of payment is the point.

faqs.question: What if we cannot list every procedure?
faqs.answer: List the visits people book first, with what is included and what is billed separately. A first visit, a follow-up, and a common add-on are more useful than a spreadsheet of codes. Link a longer schedule if you have one that stays accurate. Do not hide the first-visit fee behind the spreadsheet.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small clinic pricing page is where an anxious patient judges fit. They are asking whether they can afford to walk in, what the visit covers, and how to book. They are not there to build a spreadsheet.

Show what is included, what is not, and the shape of the fee. If the front desk would answer the question on the phone, the page should answer it too. Hiding a knowable price does not feel premium. It feels like the surprise is waiting in the room.

## Fit, before the arithmetic

A patient who is already worried will use the fee to decide whether this clinic is even a candidate. Sticker shock in the chair is a worse moment than sticker shock at home. The page exists so the shock, if there is one, happens before they have taken time off work.

Lead with the visit they are most likely to book. Usually that is a first visit. Say how long it is, who they see, and what the fee covers. One block, readable without a legend. If you have a second common visit, put it next to the first in the same pattern. Do not open with a paragraph about your commitment to transparency. The numbers are the transparency.

Nielsen Norman Group notes that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. A pricing page written as an essay will be skimmed and then distrusted, because the fee was in a sentence they skipped. Put the figure, or the honest shape, where a scan lands. Use the prose to say what the figure means.

Google's helpful-content questions ask whether a reader will leave feeling they must search again for a better answer. "Call us for fees" on a first visit you quote every day forces that second search, or a phone call the patient was not ready to make. The call can remain for anything that truly varies. It should not be the only way to learn the price of walking through the door.

## What the fee includes

Inclusion is the visit, described as the patient will experience it. Time with the clinician. The examination that is part of that time. A written note, if you provide one. A short plan for what happens next. Use the words your clinicians use in the room, then check they are words a new patient knows.

Be concrete about time. "Up to 40 minutes with the clinician" is different from "a consultation." An anxious patient is also an employee, a parent, or someone in pain who needs to know the shape of the hour. If the visit sometimes runs long, say what you do. You finish the conversation, or you book a follow-up. Do not leave them imagining they will be rushed out, and do not promise a length you do not keep.

If a coordinator, a therapist, and a clinician are all in the fee, name the sequence. Who they meet first matters as much as the total. A fee that says "comprehensive assessment" and does not say who is in the room is a brochure line. The room is the product.

Group inclusions as a short list under the figure, not as a footnote. Three to six lines. More than that and you are describing a package nobody can hold in mind. If the list needs a code, keep the code for the invoice and keep the list in ordinary language.

## What is billed separately

The separate list is how you keep the first number believable. Labs, imaging, a procedure you might recommend after the exam, a letter to another clinician, a product you sell, a report for an insurer. If it is not in the visit fee, say so beside the visit fee.

Write these lines without apology and without a sales push. "Imaging, if it is needed, is booked separately and quoted before you agree." That sentence respects the patient. "Additional services may apply" does not. It is the sentence people have learned to fear.

Say who quotes the extra. The clinician in the room, the desk before they leave, a written estimate. An anxious patient wants to know they will not discover a second fee at the card machine with a queue behind them. Your process is part of the price.

If you never charge extras on a first visit, say that too. A boundary can be generous. "The first visit fee includes the examination and the plan. We do not add a fee for the written note." Specific generosity is more calming than a vague promise of care.

## The shape of the price

Publish the number when you have one. A first visit that is always the same fee should show the fee, the currency, and whether tax is included if that is how you invoice. A range is right when the range is real: a short visit and a long visit, labeled by what each is for.

If insurance changes what the patient pays, show both shapes without pretending to know their benefits.

- Self-pay: the fee for the visit.
- Insured: whether you bill the plan directly, and what the patient might still pay, such as a copay you are allowed to describe in general terms.
- What you need from them: the card, the referral, the authorization, if you require it.

Do not list twenty insurers unless someone owns that list and reviews it when a plan changes. A stale "we accept everyone" line is worse than "bring your card and we will tell you before the visit what we can bill." Currency and honesty beat coverage theater.

Cancellation belongs on this page. The notice you need, and the fee if there is one. Patients who are anxious cancel, and they should know the rule before they book. A cancellation fee revealed in a confirmation email they did not read is a fight you can avoid. State it in the same plain type as the visit fee.

## How to book from the price

Every fee block needs a way to book that visit. The button should name the visit, not say "Enquire." If online booking can attach the right appointment type, use it. If a human must confirm because the fee depends on a question, say that the booking is a request and the desk will confirm the fee before the day. Then keep that promise.

Do not make them reconstruct the fee in a contact form. "Reason for visit" is fair. A grid of codes is not. Pass the visit type they already chose into the booking so they do not select it twice. Double entry feels like a test. Tests feel like the clinic is not ready for someone who is tired.

Put the phone number on the page as a peer to the button. A patient who wants the fee repeated by a person should get a person. The person should quote the same figure the page shows. If the desk and the page disagree, stop booking until they agree. A pricing page is an operational document that happens to be public.

Hanabi's selected work is a record of pages that make one decision obvious. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is worth a look if you are about to hide the fee under a textured hero. The useful standard is legibility. A patient should be able to read the number and the next step without learning your brand voice first.

## A page the desk can stand behind

Read the page aloud at the front desk. Every sentence the staff would contradict needs a rewrite or a change in how you charge. The page cannot be a marketing version of a different fee schedule. One schedule, two surfaces.

Ask a patient who recently booked, if they are willing, what they wish they had known about cost. Add that line. Delete a line nobody has asked about in a year. Pricing pages grow stale by accumulation: old packages, a promotion that ended, a clinician who left whose visit type is still for sale.

Date the schedule in ordinary language when fees change. "Fees current as of this season" is enough if you also change the numbers. Do not leave last year's first-visit fee up because the photograph is hard to edit. On a Hanabi project the page is built so the words can change without a redesign, in the repository the clinic owns. A fee you cannot update is a fee you should not have published.

Keep the legal sentence your counsel wants, and keep it after the human sentence. The human sentence is "a first visit is this fee and includes this hour." The legal sentence can define exceptions. It should not be the only sentence.

## What not to do with the fee

Do not anchor a low "from" price that nobody books. A ten-minute phone call priced as the headline, with the real visit three times higher and unexplained, is a bait. Anxious patients feel bait more sharply than casual shoppers. They are already braced for a trick.

Do not compare yourself to a hospital charge or a competitor's charge unless you can show the comparison fairly and you are willing to maintain it. A slash through a number you never charged is theater. Theater is the tone this page exists to avoid.

Do not add a countdown or a "limited assessments this month" banner unless the diary is actually closed and the page explains how the waitlist works. Scarcity on a clinic fee feels like pressure. Pressure is not a bedside manner.

Once the fee is readable, the patient still needs the work described as jobs, not as a tariff. [The services page a small clinic actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-small-clinic-actually-needs) is the next piece: each visit in the patient's language, with an outcome, a boundary, and a way to book.
